_doc: Unit catalogue for ledger.mjs init. Every tracked file goes to the first unit (in order) one of whose rules matches it, unless an exclude pattern matches first. tests: null means the top-level tests pattern sorts the unit's files into SOURCE and TESTS. Text fields may use {{LEDGER}}, {{SNAPSHOT}}, {{BASE}}, {{CHECKOUT}}, {{WORKTREES}}; SP in them means the ledger, as the reviewer brief defines it.

units.what: the in-house headless tiling engine (Lath) and its React host.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/tiling-engine.md` and `docs/specs/tiling-engine.rationale.md`; skim `docs/specs/glossary.md` for vocabulary and the parts of `docs/specs/layout.md` that the engine serves (minimize/reattach, zoom). Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: The pure split-tree core: invariants after every operation (split, remove, move, resize, swap, minimize/restore), ratio sums and rounding drift, minimum sizes, degenerate trees (single leaf, empty, deeply nested), id stability.
The never-re-parent guarantee in `LathHost.tsx`: a pane's DOM node must never be re-parented (xterm canvases and iframes reload). Find any path that remounts or re-parents a pane.
Persistence round trip of layouts: serialize → restore, malformed or older persisted trees, unknown leaf ids, what happens when restore meets fewer or more surfaces than leaves.
The drag controller: drop on self, cancel mid-drag (Escape, pointer-capture loss, window blur), stale drop targets after layout changes during a drag, listeners left attached.
The wall store and engine: subscription granularity, work done per pointer move or per resize frame, `ResizeObserver` loops, tween cancellation and leftover animation frames.
Dead code: exported operations nothing calls, options never passed, tests pinning behavior no caller uses.

units.what: the Workspace model (`Window ⊃ Workspace ⊃ Pane ⊃ Surface`): the workspace store and UI store, lifecycle, control, transfer of surfaces between Workspaces, the WorkspaceStrip with its drag and motion code, auto-naming, and the window session aggregator.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): the Workspace sections of `docs/specs/layout.md` + `layout.rationale.md`, the workspace parts of `docs/specs/reopen.md`, the Workspace union projection in `docs/specs/alert.md`, and `docs/specs/glossary.md` (invariants I1–I10). Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: Moving a Surface between Workspaces: the id must stay stable, the PTY must survive, alerts and TODO state must follow, dirty or pending Tools and iframes must be refused or handled as the spec says. Look for a path where a move drops or duplicates a surface, or leaves it in two Workspaces.
Closing or killing a Workspace that holds running work, the active Workspace, or the last Workspace; what `--force` paths skip; what Reopen restores.
Workspace ids: `workspace:<n>` counters must be durable and never reused. Name collisions (`workspace:<name>`, a Workspace literally named `new`).
Strip drag-reorder and tab tweens: cancel paths, stale indices after a concurrent change, listeners and animation frames left behind.
Auto-naming: when it runs, what it reads, and whether it can overwrite a user's rename.
The window session aggregator (standalone has several windows): ordering, a window closing mid-aggregate, work repeated per change.
Persistence of Workspace order and the active Workspace across restart.
Dead code and duplicated logic between `workspace-control.ts`, `workspace-lifecycle.ts`, `workspace-transfer.ts`, and `surface-move.ts`.

units.what: session persistence and restore, terminal lifecycle and registry, id pools, reconnect, Reopen and the close paths, pending (delayed) kills, the host-side recovery capture and store, atomic JSON files, and the small `canopy/` WebGL lab.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): the session-lifecycle and persistence-recovery sections of `docs/specs/layout.md`, all of `docs/specs/reopen.md` + rationale, the persisted-session types and reconnection parts of `docs/specs/transport.md`, `docs/compatible-agents.md` + `docs/compatible-agents.rationale.md` (the hidden recovery contract: shutdown capture, detection, single-use records, cold-restore execution), and `docs/specs/webgl-text.md` for `canopy/` and `terminal-webgl.ts`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: Save → restore round trips: what is lost, malformed or truncated persisted data, older shapes, a restore that meets missing PTYs, and writes that race a quit. Persisted formats have reached early users, so treat format changes as `Sure-fix: no`.
Id pools and surface ids: counters must be durable and never reused, including across a crash between allocating and saving.
Reopen: stack order and limits, reopening after the Workspace or window that held the surface is gone, single-use guarantees.
Pending kills: the delayed-kill timer, undo, app quit or window close while a kill is pending, a second kill of the same surface, which surface actually dies.
Reconnect: backoff, duplicate sessions after a reconnect, buffered output replay ordering, listeners that accumulate per reconnect.
Terminal lifecycle: dispose order, xterm instances or listeners that leak when a pane closes, WebGL context loss and the browser's context limit, the fallback renderer path.

Recovery capture and store on the host: single-use records, timestamps that can be `NaN`, files left behind, what an attacker-controlled terminal title or command can inject into a resume command line (`resume-patterns.ts`, `coding-agents.ts`).
`atomic-json-file.ts` and `local-json-store.ts`: rename atomicity, fsync, Windows behavior, concurrent writers.
Dead code: compatibility branches for shapes nothing writes, unused helpers.

units.what: the Activity layer: `alert-manager.ts` (1,454 lines), delivery scheduling and policy, alert settings, speech (local engine, speech queue, managed voice engine and its host), quiesce detection, watched commands, presence and engagement, TODO spotlight, push devices, the alert ring and TODO pill components, and the host-side alert protocol (`alert-host.ts`, `alert-client.ts`, `alert-protocol.ts`, `managed-voice-host.ts`).
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/alert.md` + `docs/specs/alert.rationale.md`. The maintainer treats the state-machine diagrams in `alert.md` as the **complete model**: every transition the code makes must be an edge in a diagram, and every edge must exist in code. Check both directions, edge by edge, and list each mismatch as its own finding. Also read the notification-protocol rows in `docs/specs/terminal-escapes.md`.
focus: The attention model and TODO lifecycle: transitions that can strand a session ringing forever, drop a completion the user never saw, or ring for output the user was watching. `attend()` historically conflated acknowledgement, presence, and focus; check what is left of that.

Notification protocols and their sanitization rules: terminal output is attacker-controlled, so trace every byte from an OSC notification to the DOM, to speech text, to push payloads, and to OS notifications.

Timers: the delivery scheduler, quiesce detector, speech queue, and presence each own timers. Find ones that are never cleared on session kill, Workspace close, or unmount, and work done per PTY chunk.
Speech: queue ordering, cancellation, a managed-voice failure falling back (or not), token and error handling in `managed-voice-host.ts`, audio that keeps playing after the alert is dismissed.
Watched commands and `await` (the `dor await` absorb path): alerts absorbed that the user should have received, or delivered twice.
Push devices: stale device records, payload contents.
The Workspace union projection: a Workspace tab showing a state none of its sessions hold.
Dead code: settings nothing reads, alert tracks or states no transition reaches, the retired bell.

units.what: per-Session semantic state: `terminal-state.ts` (1,609 lines), its store, `terminal-protocol.ts` (1,091 lines), the processed PTY stream, the report filter, OSC sanitization, the keyboard-protocol arbiter, prompt and command lifecycle, shell store and escaping, the helper terminal and unified terminal context views, and the host-side git info helpers.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/terminal-state.md`, `docs/specs/terminal-context.md`, `docs/specs/terminal-escapes.md`, each with its `.rationale.md`. `terminal-escapes.md` is a registry: every sequence the code parses, answers, or ignores must have a row, and every row must match code. Check both directions and list each mismatch.
focus: Parsing across chunk boundaries: an OSC, CSI, DCS, or APC split between two PTY chunks, an unterminated sequence that grows a buffer without bound, ST vs BEL terminators, 8-bit C1 controls, invalid UTF-8.

Terminal output is attacker-controlled (`cat` of a hostile file, `curl`, an SSH session). Trace titles, cwd reports, command text, hyperlinks, and notifications to wherever they land: the DOM, a shell command line, a file path, a git spawn, the clipboard. `osc-sanitize.ts`, `shell-escape.ts`, and `posix-escape.ts` must hold for POSIX shells, fish, cmd.exe, and PowerShell.

`terminal-report-filter.ts`: replies to queries (DA, DSR, color queries, XTVERSION, kitty keyboard) must never let program output inject keyboard input, and must not be answered twice (once by xterm.js and once by Dormouse).
`keyboard-protocol-arbiter.ts`: push/pop balance, state after a program crashes without popping, state across reconnect.
Prompt and command lifecycle (OSC 133/633 and friends): states that get stuck, command text mis-attributed, title and header derivation and grouping keys.
The helper terminal: lifecycle, promotion, source closure, as `terminal-context.md` states them.
Host git helpers: how often git is spawned (per cwd change? per render?), timeouts, a cwd that is deleted, huge repos, paths with spaces or newlines.
Per-chunk cost: regexes that can backtrack on long lines, repeated string concatenation of large buffers, state recomputed for every chunk.
Dead code: parsed fields nothing reads, protocol branches no shell integration script emits (compare with `standalone/sidecar/shell-integration/`).

units.what: terminal-owned selection, the copy editor (Auto / Exact / Spaces / No breaks), paste tiers, smart URL and path extension, external-link confirmation, clipboard write and failure handling, and the mouse-ownership router.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/mouse-and-clipboard.md` + its rationale, and the terminal-output and paste sections of `docs/specs/security-local.md`. The spec includes a mouse-ownership state matrix: check every cell against `terminal-mouse-router.ts`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: `copy-text.ts`: each mode's output for wrapped lines, trailing spaces, wide characters, emoji, combining marks, tabs, box-drawing, prompts, and the per-break marks. Look for off-by-one at line and selection boundaries and for selections that span scrollback.
Selection across resize and reflow (`selection-reflow.ts`, `selection-geometry.ts`): a selection that points at the wrong cells after the terminal reflows or scrolls.
Paste: a paste must never smuggle the bracketed-paste end marker or other control characters, in any tier, on any host. Check the confirm tiers and what counts as "dangerous".
OSC 52 and program-driven clipboard writes: size limits, invalid base64, whether a program can write the clipboard silently, the "From <program>" attribution.
Smart tokens: URL and path extension with IPv6 literals, trailing punctuation, parentheses, Windows paths, `file:` URLs, and paths with spaces.
External links: scheme allowlist, IDN and homograph display, userinfo in URLs, what the confirmation actually shows versus what opens.
`redact-high-entropy.ts`: false negatives on common secret shapes and where redaction is applied.
The copy editor component: focus and keyboard handling (`f`/`e`/arrow keys), placement off-screen, listeners left attached, edits lost on resize.
Mouse-mode programs (vim, tmux, htop): ownership handoff, the override banner, a stuck drag after pointer-capture loss.
Dead code and duplicated helpers across the `selection-*` and `clipboard*` files.

units.what: the webview side of the browser Surface: `agent-browser-surface-controller.ts` (1,955 lines), the agent-browser panel, screen modal, connection and screen modules, `IframePanel.tsx` (784 lines), browser URL and port helpers, binding reservations, dev-server port detection, and iframe policy.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): the webview-side sections of `docs/specs/dor-browser.md` + `docs/specs/dor-browser.rationale.md`, and the browser-pane sections of `docs/specs/security-local.md`. The host side (`lib/src/host/`) belongs to the `browser-host` unit; read it only to follow a call. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: The surface controller as a state machine: every state and transition for connect, launch, tab change, pop-out to a window and back, reconnect, and close. Look for states it cannot leave, a screencast that stays bound to an old tab after the browser changes tabs on its own, and URL or tab state lost in a pop-in or pop-out.
Binding and port reservations: reservations that leak when a launch fails or a surface closes mid-launch; two surfaces claiming one key.
Input forwarding: coordinate scaling with device pixel ratio, zoom, and viewport presets; modifier keys; wheel deltas; IME composition; focus theft from the terminal.

`IframePanel.tsx`: the `sandbox` and `allow` attributes, `postMessage` handlers that do not check `event.origin` or `event.source`, navigation tracking, the proxy URL it builds, reload behavior on re-render or re-parent, the `https://` refusal.
`use-dev-server-ports.ts`: how often it polls, what each poll costs on the host, whether it stops when no pane needs it.
URL handling (`browser-url.ts`, `port-url.ts`): `:5173`, `host:port`, IPv6, userinfo, `javascript:` and `data:` URLs.
Listeners, timers, sockets, and object URLs that outlive the surface; frames decoded but never shown; base64 or image decode work per frame.
Dead code: render modes, providers, or controller branches nothing selects.

units.what: the Node-side browser stack bundled into both hosts: the iframe proxy and its rewriter, the agent-browser host, the generic browser host, the browser viewer, the Playwright host and installer, browser sync, capture and capture budget, launch environment, the loopback guard, the private capture directory, and the replay buffer.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): the host-side sections of `docs/specs/dor-browser.md` + `docs/specs/dor-browser.rationale.md`, and in `docs/specs/security-local.md` the "Loopback Listeners", "Browser panes", and "Network policy" sections with their `FAIL IF` lines. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: The iframe proxy: it must reach only the loopback targets the spec allows. Look for SSRF (redirects, `Host` header tricks, DNS rebinding, IPv6 and decimal-IP forms, a target that resolves off-box), request smuggling, header and CSP rewriting mistakes, cookies crossing between proxied origins, WebSocket upgrade handling, streaming and backpressure, and sockets or servers that are never closed on error.
`iframe-proxy-rewrite.ts`: HTML and header rewriting on chunk boundaries, compressed bodies, huge bodies, non-UTF-8 content.
A loopback bind is not an access control: every listener here must check its guard. Find a listener or route that skips `loopback-guard.ts` or its token.

Process lifecycle in `agent-browser-host.ts`, `browser-host.ts`, and `playwright-host.ts`: spawn failures, zombie or orphaned browser and daemon processes after a host crash or surface close, kill escalation, per-surface state directories, concurrent commands against one browser, Windows differences. The neutral cwd and launch environment: what leaks into the browser's environment.
Capture: the capture budget, private capture directory permissions and cleanup, files left behind, frame buffers that grow.
`playwright-install.ts`: what it downloads or runs, and on whose say-so.
Synchronous filesystem or subprocess calls on a hot path; work done per frame.
Dead code: hosts, providers, or options nothing constructs. The two test files `file-viewer-proxy.test.ts` and `folder-viewer-proxy.test.ts` have no same-named source: say what they actually test.

units.what: the webview side of the `dor` control socket: `use-dor-control.ts` (2,538 lines), `dor-control-router.ts`, `dor-control-shared.ts`, and `app-control.ts`. The unit is small on purpose: read it slowly, and read the wire contract it must honor in `dor/src/protocol.ts` and `dor/src/control-methods.ts`, plus the callers of each method in `dor/src/commands/`.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/dor-cli.md` + its rationale, for control-socket plumbing, the Surface handle model, and the command set; and the control-verb parts of `docs/specs/dor-tool.md` and `docs/specs/dor-browser.md`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: The method table: every method the CLI can send has a handler, and every handler has a CLI caller. List methods on one side only.

Reply discipline: every request gets exactly one reply on every path, including thrown errors, a surface killed mid-request, a Workspace closed mid-request, and a client that disconnects while waiting. Find hung requests and double replies.

Handle resolution: `surface:N`, `surface:self`, `surface:focused`, `title:<exact>`, `workspace:<n>`, `workspace:<name>`. Look for a stale or reused id retargeting a destructive verb (`kill`, `send`), helper terminals leaking into listings or matching, and Workspace scoping mistakes (`--workspace`, `--all`).
`ensure`: the command + cwd identity key, matching against live commands, `--restart` keeping layout place, races between two simultaneous `ensure` calls creating duplicates.
`await`: `--until quiet` and `--until exit` semantics, waiter cleanup on kill or disconnect, alert absorption, timeouts.
`send`: text, key, stdin, and sequence modes; pacing; what happens to a queue when the target dies.
`kill --confirm-if-read`: what text is compared and whether it can match the wrong thing.
`move`, `reopen`, `workspace` verbs, and `app restart`.
Caller identity and authority: which caller may target which Workspace or window, and what an unauthenticated or forged caller id can do.
Dead code inside the 2,538-line hook: handlers, helpers, or fields nothing reaches; duplicated resolution logic that should be one function.

units.what: Dor Tools: the `tool` Surface (a terminal and a browser on one Session spine), on both sides. Webview: tool control, navigation, takeover, transfer, the reaper, serving detection, run-end, the Tool panel and header, approval, port conflict, the preview slot and its transitions. Host: the tool registry, trust, tool host, input, open rules, user config, listing. Plus the whole `dor-tools-lib/` package (the MIT Tool-protocol library).
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/dor-tool.md` + rationale, `docs/specs/dor-tools-lib.md`, and the Tool and trust sections of `docs/specs/security-local.md`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: Trust: a project's `dormouse.yml` must run nothing until the user approves it. What exactly is approved (path, content hash, per Tool?), what invalidates approval, and whether anything can run a project Tool between an edit and re-approval. Comments in the file describe; they never authorize.

The OSC 367 contract and the launch latch: who may announce a port, when, how many times, and what a hostile program inside the terminal can make the pane do (flip to a browser of an arbitrary port or URL, steal a key, relaunch).
Registry and config parsing: malformed YAML, unknown fields, `run` as string vs list, `$HERE` expansion, `prespawn_dedupe` keys colliding across checkouts, viewport values.
Serving detection and port conflict; the terminal ↔ browser flip in both directions with a stable id; `[keyed]` re-run semantics (`existing`, `adopted`, `--fresh`).
Takeover and transfer between Workspaces; dirty and pending Tools refusing a move.
The reaper: it must kill only processes it owns. Find a path that kills the wrong process or leaves the Tool's children running.
The iframe save channel in `dor-tools-lib`: origin and source checks, message validation.
The preview slot: one reusable preview per Workspace, replace without stealing focus, transitions that strand a pane.
`dor-tools-lib`: the license and dependency boundary the spec states (MIT, no runtime dependencies), its entry points, and exports nothing uses.
Dead code and stores that duplicate each other (`tool-*-store.ts`).

units.what: the mobile composition: `MobileTerminalUi.tsx` (1,261 lines), `MobileWall.tsx`, the radial gesture menu (component and `mobile-gesture-menu.ts`), mobile scroll, font size, the Type composer, the Sessions screen and its Settings, the mobile browser pane and close dialog.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/mobile-terminal-ui.md` + rationale. It ships in the website's Pocket playground and in the Pocket app. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: Touch handling: gesture recognition thresholds, a gesture that starts as a scroll and becomes a menu (or the reverse), multi-touch, pointer-cancel, `touch-action` and passive-listener mistakes that block or double-fire, the dual-tap detector. Say for each finding whether your evidence is simulated event ordering or native behavior.

The on-screen keyboard: the terminal is panned above the keyboard using the visual viewport. Look for resize loops, a stale pan after rotation or keyboard dismissal, and iOS Safari versus Android Chrome differences the code assumes away.
The Type composer: text lost on blur or orientation change, IME composition and autocorrect, Enter versus newline, paste, what is sent to the PTY and when.
The radial menu: actions that fire on the wrong session after a session switch, items whose handlers are missing, geometry at screen edges and with safe-area insets.
Scrolling: momentum scroll fighting xterm's own scrolling, scroll position lost on output, cost per touchmove.
The Sessions screen and Settings: state that disagrees with the desktop Wall for the same sessions; close and kill confirmation targeting.
Listeners, timers, and observers left attached after unmount; work per frame.
Dead code: gesture modes, menu entries, or props nothing uses; desktop-only code paths reachable here by mistake.

units.what: the rest of the laptop-side remote stack and its Settings UI: `one-time-runtime.ts` (861 lines) and its store, enrollment, activation, passkey sync, pairing approval and the pairing modal, the enrolled gate, the Burrow status store, the network-policy store and `network-policy.ts`, the one-time rendezvous client, `ws.ts`, and the Settings components (`RemoteControlSection.tsx` at 1,165 lines, `NetworkSettings.tsx`, `PairedDevices.tsx`, `HostedEnrollment.tsx`, `OneTimeConnection.tsx`, the Baseboard indicator, QR and scannable-code components).
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/one-time.md` + rationale, `docs/specs/remote-network.md` + rationale (Nowhere / Local networks only / Anywhere / Anywhere through your Relay: the choke points, the update reminder, the Local networks path check), the enrollment and "Settings → Remote control" sections of `docs/specs/relay.md`, the pairing sections of `docs/specs/remote-security-model.md`, and `docs/stories/pairing.mdx`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: The network policy as a choke point: every level must actually stop what it claims to stop. Find a path (a reconnect timer, a status poll, an enrollment check, an update reminder) that reaches the network at "Nowhere", or reaches beyond the local network at "Local networks only". A policy change while connected must take effect at once.

One-time connection: the link's lifetime and single use, the two-digit confirm, direct-only (the session must never fall back through Hosted), nothing saved, no resume; what a second scanner of the same QR gets; teardown on the laptop when the panel closes.

Pairing approval: what the user is shown before approving, an approval that outlives a user-verification requirement being raised, an approval dialog for one device answered while another request arrives, a stale modal.

Enrollment and activation: device-code flow states, retry and expiry, a token or setup password kept longer than needed or logged, switching between Hosted and a self-host Relay origin (the rule: one relay origin; non-default means self-host and nothing reaches dormouse.sh).
Passkey sync and removal: removing a passkey must end that passkey's sessions.
The status store: status that can disagree with reality (shows "connected" after the socket died), subscription churn.

The Settings UI: every control wired to something real, disabled and error states, copy that states something false, a destructive action (unpair, reset) with the wrong target after the list re-sorts.
`ws.ts`: the shared socket surface: close and error handling, backoff, listeners that accumulate.
Dead code: Settings sections, store fields, or runtime branches nothing reaches.

units.what: the laptop-side remote session in `lib/src/remote/burrow/`: `burrow-runtime.ts` (2,148 lines), `established-session.ts`, `remote-api.ts`, `frame-tunnel.ts`, peer surfaces, the surface provider, directory collection, the ACL, the access log, push delivery, `burrow-fetch.ts`, embedded pages, client close and take-back.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/remote-api.md` + rationale (the shipped terminal-only protocol-v1 and what is staged), `docs/specs/remote-security-model.md` + rationale (one Noise channel per ceremony, per-Burrow Client statics, the Burrow authorizes the pair, not the Relay), and the Burrow rows of `docs/specs/security-remote.md`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: Authorization at the Burrow: every protocol-v1 request from a Client must be checked against the ACL and the session's presence state before it touches a PTY. Find a request type that skips a check, a check done on Relay-supplied data instead of the Noise-authenticated identity, and state that survives a revocation or passkey removal (live sessions must end).
The ACL writer: the spec says exactly one. Ordering between "ACL saved" and "pair is live".

Session establishment and teardown in `burrow-runtime.ts`: a second ceremony for the same Client, a Client that vanishes mid-ceremony, resume, displaced sessions, timers and maps that grow per connection.

Message handling: every inbound frame is size-bounded and validated before use; unknown types; replay or reordering inside a session; what a malicious Relay can cause (it can drop, delay, and reorder ciphertext but must learn and forge nothing).
`remote-api.ts`: which surfaces a Client can see and act on, input and resize routing to the right PTY, output replay bounds, what crosses the boundary (titles, cwd, clipboard, alerts).
`frame-tunnel.ts` and embedded pages (remote iframes and Tools on the phone): which origins and ports can be reached, header handling, body size limits, SSRF through the tunnel.
`burrow-fetch.ts`: it must use the guarded transport and honor the network policy with no global fallback.
Push delivery: what is in a push payload, endpoint validation (no re-parsing a stored endpoint into a different host), rate limits.
The access log: what it records, growth bounds, sensitive content.
Dead code: staged protocol branches that are wired but unreachable, message types nothing sends.

units.what: the Pocket app shell (`lib/src/remote/pocket-app/`: `App.tsx` at 1,475 lines, the scan-invitation flow, the Pocket wall and browser frame, views, the service worker, deployment and pair-link helpers), the one-time phone page (`lib/src/remote/one-time-app/`), the static shells under `lib/pocket/` and `lib/one-time/`, the diagnostics pages, and the Pocket, service-worker, and one-time Vite configs.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): `docs/specs/pocket-app.md` + rationale (the remote session is a `PlatformAdapter`, so Pocket is auth screens plus the mobile composition; the same-origin deployment rule), the phone-page sections of `docs/specs/one-time.md` + rationale, and the Pocket rows of `docs/specs/security-remote.md`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
focus: `App.tsx` as a state machine: sign-in, pairing, reconnect, session list, session view, sign-out, passkey removal. States it cannot leave, a spinner with no timeout, an error that is swallowed, a stale session shown after the Burrow revokes the phone.

The service worker (`sw.ts`, `service-worker.ts`, `sw-entry.ts`): cache versioning and update flow (a stale app shell pinned forever), what is cached (never credentials or session data), push event handling and notification click targets, scope. The spec says no checked-in built service worker.
The scan-invitation flow: QR parsing, camera permission denial, a malformed or hostile invitation link, what is shown to the user before they accept.
Stored state: what lives in IndexedDB or localStorage, private keys (must be non-extractable if the spec says so), cleanup on sign-out. The one-time page must keep no store at all.
The one-time page: the take-link parsing, the two-digit confirm, the direct-only session, no resume; what happens on reload or a second tab.
The browser frame (`PocketBrowserFrame.tsx`, `frame-salt.ts`): origin isolation of remote iframes, `postMessage` origin checks.
Deployment (`deployment.ts`): same-origin rule, what differs between Hosted and self-host.
The diagnostics pages: reachable in production? Do they expose anything?
iOS Safari and installed-PWA specifics the code relies on (push needs a Home Screen install).
Dead code: views, routes, or branches nothing reaches; leftovers of removed flows.

units.what: the phone-side protocol in `lib/src/remote/client/`: `pocket-client.ts` (1,640 lines), `session-core.ts`, `one-time-client.ts`, `pocket-db.ts`, `frame-client.ts`, `remote-adapter.ts` (the `RemotePtyAdapter`), WebAuthn, push subscription, and the private-key store.
units.read: **Specs you own** (read first, in the snapshot): the Client side of `docs/specs/remote-api.md` + rationale and of `docs/specs/remote-security-model.md` + rationale, the adapter sections of `docs/specs/pocket-app.md`, and the Client rows of `docs/specs/security-remote.md`. Report spec-vs-code disagreements in both directions.
